sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
sections.text: Effective hate speech moderation must address explainability and bias alongside raw classification accuracy. We argue that model decisions should be accompanied by human-readable rationales —short spans of the input text that justify the assigned label—ensuring that predictions are auditable and robust. In this paper, we present Ex- HateQA, an Explainable Hate Speech Detection framework featuring Question Answering-style rationale span generation. Ex-HateQA is a parameter-efficient hybrid encoder–LLM architecture that predicts (label, rationale) tuples by formulating explanation generation as an extractive question answering (QA) task. Ex-HateQA fol­ lows the principle of parameter-efficient adaptation strategy rather than the absolute size of the underlying 7B LLM backbone. The LLM remains frozen and is updated exclusively through low-rank adapters (LoRA/QLoRA), yielding a minimal trainable parameter budget (approximately < 1% of the backbone) while preserving high generation quality for extractive, copy-only rationales. The encoder pathway performs Mask-Guided Rationale Extraction (MGRE) and multi-label prediction, while the LLM pathway generates rationale spans under a strict copy-only constraint, ensuring that the output is either a verbatim substring of the post or < unknown > . It is worth mentioning that here rather than claiming an absolute theorem of causal faithfulness, Ex-HateQA is de­ signed to encourage decision–evidence consistency : sufficiency and comprehensiveness losses regularize the encoder toward counterfactually informative rationales, and an optional alignment objective encourages agreement be­ tween MGRE token salience and the LLM’s extractive spans. We further introduce LLM-aware probes— masked prompting for counterfactual sensitivity analysis and optional rationale-tagged prompting —and optimize the model using contrastive (negative) questions to mitigate reliance on spurious triggers. Across two rigorous benchmarks, HateXplain (single-label) and CAVES (multi-label), Ex-HateQA advances the state of the art while preserving a low-latency label-screening path and a selectively invoked rationale-generation path. On HateXplain, Ex-HateQA achieves an F1 score of 0 . 7445 (a 7 . 2% improvement over the best encoder baseline) and leads span generation with a ROUGE-2 score of 0 . 4235 and a BLEU score of 0 . 5169 . Furthermore, it attains the highest subgroup robustness on GMB-Sub. and GMB-BNSP, indicating a significant reduction in bias toward target communities. Overview Social media platforms such as Facebook, Threads, and X (formerly Twitter) have become indispensable sources for acquiring real-time information across the globe. However, these platforms also host numer­ ous instances of harmful discourse, including hate speech [ 1 ], conspiracy theories, and even anti-vaccine misinformation prevalent during the COVID-19 era [ 2 , 3 ]. The proliferation of online hate marginalizes tar­ geted demographic groups and poses severe threats to human rights. The societal impact of such hostility ranges from psychological distress to the exacerbation of real-world violence. In detecting potentially harmful content—such as hate speech [ 4 , 5 ]—that adversely impacts the public, there is a demand for transparent explanations for model predictions. Automated classification systems are frequently deployed by social me­ dia platforms to identify and eliminate damaging content. However, these systems are susceptible to misclassifications; notably, innocuous messages are frequently erroneously flagged due to the mere presence of specific ‘trigger-words’. 1 Prior research has predominantly concentrated on categorizing various forms of harmful or unreliable information [ 6 ], often without offering justifications for the assigned labels. The opaque decision-making processes of these models raise significant concerns re­ garding their practical deployability [ 7 ], as raw label predictions may lack reliability in the absence of corresponding explanatory evidence. A limited number of studies [ 1 , 3 ] have attempted to extract explanatory spans directly from the input text, while others have explored generat­ ing explanations from external sources [ 8 , 9 ]. Consequently, to mitigate the societal repercussions of online hostility, robust content moderation is essential, and providing justifications for flagged posts is a critical component of this process. In addition, regulatory frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation mandate a ‘right to explana­ tion’, 2 further necessitating the development of interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) models. The primary objective of this research is to extract ‘rationale’ spans, or localized text fragments, directly from the original input text, which isolate the specific linguistic features for predicting a given class by the AI models. While considerable progress has been made in developing high-accuracy classifiers based on deep learning architectures, the opac­ ity of such models presents a critical challenge. In sensitive application domains like content moderation, it is imperative not only to predict whether a post constitutes hate speech but also to provide interpretable and faithful rationales for the decision, thereby fostering transparency, accountability, and human trust. In this work, we present a novel QA-based method for multi-label explainable text classification, which is built upon prior work of MuLX- QA [ 11 ] that frames explanation extraction as an extractive question answering (QA) problem. Our contribution is a faithfulness-oriented and deployment-aware extension of this QA paradigm through a hy­ brid encoder–LLM design: we replace pointer-based span selection with an instruction-tuned LLM. The proposed approach is strictly constrained to generate only substrings of the input via a hard copy-only mask and constrained decoding. We couple this evidence generator with an MGRE-informed encoder pathway and explicit faithfulness objectives. This hybridization is designed to retain the interpretability benefits of QA-style evidence while strengthening extractiveness guarantees, au­ ditability, and causal alignment between predictions and rationales under a unified training objective. Review of literature In recent years, deep learning-based techniques have been used to study hate speech identification in great detail. However, the majority of existing systems prioritize accuracy at the expense of interpretability, resulting in black-box models that are often unsuitable for deployment in sensitive real-world applications where transparency and explainability are critical. This section provides a quick overview of significant earlier research on multi-label classification and explanation prediction, as well as how it has been applied to the analysis of social media data. We also discuss the applications of QA models in the literature. 2.1 . Multiple label categorization For many years, multi-label classification has been researched [ 33 , 34 ]. For this task, various model paradigms have been explored, in­ cluding hierarchical networks [ 35 ], sequence generation [ 36 ], trans­ formers [ 37 ], multi-task learning [ 38 ], and zero-shot learning [ 39 ]. Additionally, multi-label classification has been widely applied in a va­ riety of domain-specific applications, including image data [ 40–42 ], medical data [ 22 , 37 ], disaster mitigation domain [ 43 , 44 ], and senti­ ment/emotion detection [ 38 , 45 , 46 ]. Furthermore, models have been developed to predict labels for multilingual tweets [ 44 ]. Studies on sen­ timent analysis [ 47 , 48 ], and hate speech detection [ 49 , 50 ] have also been conducted using code-mixed data, which combines English with other languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and similar languages. The multi-label classification issue is crucial to a number of jobs in the wide field of social media. For instance, the target/category classification in the hate-speech domain is a multi-label classification problem [ 51 , 52 ]. Eleven distinct emotion categories can be classified from tweets using the SemEval-2018 Task on multi-emotion classifi­ cation [ 38 , 53 , 54 ]. Additionally, several previous studies utilize Reddit data to detect users’ interests by multi-label categorization [ 55 ]. 2.2 . Proposed approach: explainable hate speech detection framework with question answering (QA) style rationale span generation (Ex-HateQA) Recent literature has advanced rationale extraction substantially, particularly through Masked Rationale Prediction (MRP) [ 10 ] as an in­ termediate encoder task and MuLX-QA [ 11 ], which frames multi-label rationale extraction as a pointer-network-based question answering problem. The transition from these paradigms to Ex-HateQA should be understood not as a claim of absolute causal verification, but as a change in how extractive grounding and decision–evidence consistency are jointly optimized. In conventional pointer-network QA systems such as MuLX-QA, the extracted span can be highly plausible and well-bounded, yet the downstream classifier is not explicitly regularized to depend on that span. Likewise, encoder-only rationale mechanisms such as MRP improve token-level evidence selection, but they do not directly pro­ vide a generator-level grounding mechanism for human-facing span production. To address these limitations, Ex-HateQA couples an MGRE-enhanced encoder with an instruction-tuned LLM operating under a hard copy- only decoding constraint. The resulting support restriction maps the open-vocabulary generation problem to an extractive evidence-selection problem by forcing the rationale generator to select only tokens sup­ ported by the source post. This yields a deterministic guarantee of extractive grounding. In addition, the unified objective incorporates sufficiency and comprehensiveness regularizers so that the classifier is encouraged to remain predictive when rationale tokens are retained and to degrade when those tokens are removed. These mechanisms pro­ vide faithfulness-oriented training signals and counterfactual evidence of decision–evidence coupling, but they are not presented as a univer­ sal proof that the extracted rationale fully captures the model’s entire causal mechanism. Specifically, we in­ clude a special < unknown > option in the decoding space; the model is trained to produce a normal span for labels that are present in the text and < unknown > for labels that are absent. Following an overview of how we organize the tuple prediction task as a QA problem, the remainder of the section delves into detail about our proposed framework and training/inference approach. 4.1.1 . The necessity of a hybrid encoder-LLM design (beyond model size) Ex-HateQA is intended to address a structural mismatch in explain­ able hate speech detection: the explanation must be local , extractive , and faithful (i.e., sufficient to justify the decision and minimally depen­ dent on spurious cues), while the label decision is a global judgment over the post. Although they do not specifically prioritize fidelity cri­ teria, encoder-only extractive QA systems (such as MuLX-QA [ 11 ]) handle locality via pointer heads and are nonetheless susceptible to un­ clear span boundaries in noisy, informal social-media material. On the other hand, unless controlled, a free-form LLM generator is prone to non-extractive paraphrase or hallucinated evidence, yet it can generate coherent justifications. Ex-HateQA resolves this mismatch by factorizing responsibilities across two coupled components. Path-A is a calibrated discriminative encoder that learns label decisions and token salience under MGRE supervi­ sion, providing stable intermediate representations under the same fixed splits and preprocessing used for all baselines. Path-B is an instruction- tuned generator that is constrained to produce only substrings of the input via a hard vocabulary mask ( Eq. (7) , Proposition 1) and con­ strained decoding ( Algorithm 1 ), which strictly restricts the hypothesis space to extractive evidence and prevents out-of-input generations by construction. The two paths are not a loose “engineering concatena­ tion”; they are coupled through the unified objective ( Eq. 16 ), which explicitly trades off label accuracy, extractive evidence generation, and faithfulness terms (comprehensiveness/sufficiency) so that the model is optimized for decision–evidence consistency rather than for prediction alone. Lastly, Ex-HateQA is not trained as a fully optimized 7B model; in­ stead, the LLM backbone is frozen and modified via lightweight PEFT updates ( Table 14 ). This decision keeps the optimization footprint mod­ est and the explanation space confined while purposefully utilizing the LLM’s instruction-following prior for boundary-consistent span gener­ ation. Table 13 provides a high-level comparison to MuLX-QA that highlights these design differences. 4.2 . Design rationale and formal motivation Ex-HateQA may be characterized as a hybrid encoder–LLM pipeline, but its design adheres to a fundamental goal: to discourage dependence on bogus identity cues or superficial artifacts and to forecast hate-related labels while generating grounded and auditable evidence spans. Decoding configuration and temperature settings Since the QA module is limited to extractive copy-only gener­ ation ( Algorithm 1 ) and the goal is to choose verifiable evidence spans rather than sample free-form rationalizations, all published find­ ings for Ex-HateQA utilize deterministic decoding. The best F1 is obtained by Ex-HateQA with LLaMA-2 and 𝑁 =5 contrastive questions (F1 = 𝟎 . 𝟓𝟒𝟗𝟔 ; Acc = 0 . 5455 , Prec = 0 . 5526 , Rec = 0 . 5467 ), improving over the strongest encoder baseline BERT-MRP (F1 ≈0 . 4706 ) by roughly +0 . 079 abso­ lute ( ∼+16 . 48% improvement over BERT-MRP ). Increasing 𝑁 generally tightens decision boundaries and benefits multi-label tuple matching: the Qwen-2.5 backbone with 𝑁 =9 yields the highest Acc ( 0 . 5564 ), while LLaMA-2 with 𝑁 =9 attains the highest Prec ( 0 . 5568 ); Recall peaks at LLaMA-2 with 𝑁 =5 ( 0 . 5467 ). In all cases, generative encoder–decoder baselines ( Paraphrase , Unified-BART ) trail substantially. These gains corroborate the effectiveness of combining MGRE pre-finetuning with copy-only QA span generation for precise tuple-level predictions in the more challenging multi-label setting. Ex-HateQA significantly outperforms BERT-RP and BERT-MRP on CAVES. A recognized drawback of exclusively encoder-side reasoning pretrain­ ing is seen in the little improvement from BERT-RP to BERT-MRP on CAVES: Token salience calibration is improved by MGRE-style inter­ mediate supervision, but tuple-level scoring on CAVES necessitates the simultaneous fulfillment of (i) accurate label selection and (ii) sufficiently overlapping span boundaries within an IOU threshold. When stringent IOU restrictions are applied, discriminative token heads typically over- extend spans to secure the classification choice, which might preserve label-F1 but depress tuple-level matching. In order to reduce boundary inflation and force extractive, contiguous evidence, Ex-HateQA intro­ duces a label-conditioned QA generator trained under a hard copy-only constraint. Conversely, contrastive questioning explicitly teaches the model to output < unknown > for absent labels. In multi-label contexts like CAVES, where more negative/contrastive questions increase ac­ curacy and stabilize tuple predictions, this process becomes crucial ( Section 7.13.1 , Fig. 14 ). 6.2 . In the revised manuscript, we report both the standard CAVES plausibility scores and the component-aware scores, interpreting the former as conserva­ tive historical-comparability metrics and the latter as structure-aligned auxiliary evidence. This confirms that part of the low absolute overlap observed under the standard protocol is attributable to the mismatch between a single contiguous prediction and a union-based, po­ tentially multi-fragment gold rationale. Comparison with recent baselines under distinct deployment regimes Recent explainable hate speech detection baselines differ not only in architecture but also in when explanations are produced. Some methods, such as SHIELD [ 98 ] and distillation-based XAI [ 99 ], use a large model only offline to create supervision on the training split and then deploy a compact student at inference time. Robustness and generalization under distribution shift and noise Although the major assessment in Tables 23 and 24 evaluates in- domain efficacy, practical hate-speech moderation systems must also maintain their dependability in the face of noisy inputs and distribu­ tion shifts. Topic drift, changing slang, orthographic obfuscation, emoji or punctuation variance, and code-mixed or dialectal language are some of the causes of these changes. In order to address this issue, we supple­ ment the in-domain results with a controlled robustness analysis that examines (i) sensitivity to distributional changes caused by held- out strata within the same dataset and (ii) stability under meaning- preserving textual perturbations. We measure real generalization rather than adaptation in all robustness tests by evaluating models without retraining and using the checkpoint chosen on the initial validation split. Table 33 and Fig. 7 show that moderate masking ( 0 . 30 ) typically yields the best balance: IOU F1 improves over 0 . 15 (stronger rationale learning), while sufficiency remains low (better adequacy) for CAVES dataset. At very high masking ( 0 . 50 ), comprehensiveness increases (removing predicted tokens hurts more), but tuple-F1 can plateau or slightly drop, suggesting over-regularization. However, for HateXplain dataset, higher masking ( 0 . 50 ) gives the best balance: IOU F1 improves over 0 . 30 (stronger rationale learning), while sufficiency remains low (better adequacy). Rationales behind the adoption of distinct optimal 𝑝 mask across HateXplain and CAVES. The differing optima in Table 33 (HateXplain: 𝑝 mask =0 . 50 ; CAVES: 𝑝 mask =0 . 30 ) are expected once 𝑝 mask is interpreted as a diffi­ culty and regularization knob for the MGRE intermediate task. MGRE is a conditional denoising-style objective over rationale tokens: for a post with | 𝑅 | rationale-marked tokens, the expected number of masked rationale tokens is E [ | 𝑅 masked | ] ≈ 𝑝 mask ⋅ | 𝑅 | . Increasing 𝑝 mask there­ fore (i) strengthens the pressure to infer rationale membership from broader context (stronger regularization toward contextual, human- like evidence), but simultaneously (ii) reduces the amount of direct rationale signal available per instance, potentially making the intermedi­ ate task underdetermined and causing over-regularization. The optimal 𝑝 mask is thus dataset-dependent because it depends on the redundancy, granularity, and ambiguity of the annotated rationales and on whether a single global decision or multiple label-specific decisions must be supported. HateXplain is a single-label, three-way setting (Hateful/Offensive/Normal) where arguments are usually more general and redundant with the context of the decision: evidence is often locally coherent around explicit lexical cues or brief abusive con­ structions, and multiple neighboring tokens can legitimately support the same class. While the stronger masking pressure actively discourages superficial “trigger-word” reliance by forcing the model to recover rationale membership from context and compositional semantics, a higher masking rate (here, 𝑝 mask =0 . 50 ) is still learnable in such a regime because there is still enough contextual redundancy to reconstruct masked rationale tags. This is in line with the observed improvement in fidelity behavior (lower sufficiency) and plausibility (IOU-F1) at 𝑝 mask =0 . 50 for HateXplain in Table 33 and Fig. 7 . Therefore, we provide an empirical profiling of Ex-HateQA and representative baselines in a standardized inference setup to supplement the asymptotic complexity discussion. All latency and memory measurements, unless otherwise noted, are taken on a dou­ ble NVIDIA V100 (64 GB) GPU with mixed precision, maximum input length of 128, batch size of 32, and averaged across many warm-up sessions. Ex-HateQA offers a framework for classification and detection that takes explainability and prejudice into account. We use a two-stage approach to refine a pre-trained language model. We suggested Mask-Guided Rationale Extraction (MGRE) as the intermediate task, which uses the extra rationale information of the sur­ rounding tokens to anticipate masked rationales for particular tokens. As a result, the models learn to categorize each token’s abusiveness and the context-based human reasoning process. As a consequence, the proposed model exhibits cutting-edge performance in terms of bias and explainability as well as the detection outcome in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Based on its greater explainability, the exam­ ples show how resilient it is in identifying hate speech, both explicit and implicit. In future studies, we propose applying Ex-HateQA to other do­ mains (apart from social media posts) where explanations are essential for classification. Additionally, we suggest using these models to learn more about actual social media trends in the relevant fields.

sections.text: analysis This appendix reports the contiguous-span oracle analysis previously discussed in the main text. We emphasize that this material is provided only as supplementary descriptive context. Its purpose is to illustrate how union-style rationale annotations and single-span decoding con­ straints interact under exact overlap scoring on CAVES. It is not used as the primary basis for claiming benchmark suitability or for interpreting the comparative ranking of methods in the main results. The principal interpretation of CAVES is based on the standard benchmark metrics for comparability together with the structure-aware auxiliary evaluation introduced in Section 6.3.1 . The inherently low absolute values of the IOU-F1 metric observed in our evaluations ( Table 24 )—specifically hovering in the 13 . 0% −16 . 0% range for the CAVES dataset—necessitate rigorous contextualization against the dataset’s structural curation methodology. In highly implicit, multi-label domains, exact token-boundary agreement among human annotators is notoriously sparse. As documented in the original cura­ tion of the CAVES dataset [ 3 ], human annotators exhibited significant variance in boundary delineation, prompting the dataset creators to de­ fine the final gold-standard rationale ( 𝐺 ) as the mathematical union of keyword spans selected by up to four independent annotators (i.e., 𝐺 = ⋃ 𝑘 𝑖 =1 𝐻 𝑖 , where 𝐻 𝑖 represents the tokens selected by the 𝑖 -th human annotator). This aggregation strategy inherently inflates the length and variance of the target span. Therefore, using traditional Intersection-Over-Union ( IOU = | 𝑃 ∩ 𝐺 | | 𝑃 ∪ 𝐺 | ) to assess the effectiveness of the architecture introduces an artificial dampener on absolute performance. A precise, semantically valid ra­ tionale span ( 𝑃 ) that Ex-HateQA or any other single-prediction model extracts will inevitably fulfill | 𝑃 | ≪ | 𝐺 | . The broad denominator pro­ vided by the multi-annotator union drastically limits the absolute IOU score, making scores close to 100% theoretically unachievable, even if the produced explanation fully matches the interpretation of one expert human ( 𝑃 ≈ 𝐻 1 ). Therefore, the results’ relevance is not diminished by the original literature’s lack of a specified scalar Human Upper Bound. sections.text: This appendix provides supplementary computational profiling re­ sults for the explanation path of Ex-HateQA under the standardized distributed inference setup used throughout the revised manuscript. The purpose of this appendix is to clarify how memory consumption and latency evolve as the global batch size increases under the selective rationale-generation regime. These results are reported only as supple­ mentary deployment context and are not part of the paper’s primary comparative evaluation.
